theme: I am poor and needy; you are good and forgiving
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 86. It is a prayer of David for help, based entirely on God’s goodness, not on David’s merit. Notice how many times David calls himself God’s servant.
settingTheScene: Psalm 86 is the only psalm in Book 3 attributed to David. It is a personal prayer in the middle of a series of national psalms of Asaph and the sons of Korah. The psalmist is surrounded by insolent men, but the focus is on God’s character. It takes up the language of Exodus 34:6, which you saw in Jonah: “merciful and gracious, slow to anger.” The psalm balances Isaiah’s mighty God with the personal God who hears one man.
observation: “Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy” (v. 1).
“Preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you” (v. 2).
“Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, do I lift up my soul” (v. 4).
“For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call on you” (v. 5).
“There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours” (v. 8).
“All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (v. 9).
“Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name” (v. 11).
“But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (v. 15).
interpretation:
The psalm starts with the simplest sort of prayer: “I am poor and needy.” David does not mean he lacks money. He means he has nothing that gives him a claim on God. Every request that follows rests on God’s character. “Preserve my life, for I am godly” does not boast of perfection but states his covenant loyalty. “You are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call on you.” That is the heart of the psalm. He asks because God is generous.

David repeatedly calls himself “your servant,” three times in the psalm. The word shows his posture: he belongs to God and depends on him. Being a servant means that he can ask for the master’s protection. And his daily prayer is persistent. “I cry to you all the day.”

Verses 8 to 10 widen the view: no one is like the LORD. All nations will come and worship. This echoes Isaiah 45:22-23 and the mission to the nations. Even a personal prayer is set in a universal frame.

The central request is in verse 11: “Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name.” David asks for a divided heart to be united. Anyone who has tried to follow God knows how scattered the heart can be, pulled in many directions. He prays that God would gather it into a single loyalty. It is a prayer that is worth praying every day.

Then he thanks God for deliverance from Sheol. The proud have risen against him. He asks for a sign of God’s goodness, “that those who hate me may see and be put to shame, because you, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.” The psalm moves from need to confidence, and its core is God’s self-description from Exodus 34, spoken back to him in prayer.
connection: Paul quotes Psalm 86 in the thought that all nations will worship (Romans 15:9-11, along with Psalm 18 and others). Revelation 15:4 says, “All nations will come and worship you.” Ephesians 2:4-5 speaks of God, rich in mercy. James 4:8 says, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you… purify your hearts, you double-minded.” Matthew 6:22 and Psalm 119:113 address wholeheartedness. 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 calls him the Father of mercies and God of all comfort.
application:
Pray Psalm 86:11 each morning this week: “Unite my heart to fear your name.”

Begin a prayer by admitting that you are “poor and needy,” with nothing to bring but your need.

Speak God’s own words about himself (Exodus 34:6) back to him in a prayer of trust.
prayerPrompts: Tell God that you are poor and needy.
Thank him that he is good and forgiving.
Ask him to teach you his way.
